reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with painless central blurring and distortion, and is a common cause of disappointing vision despite otherwise successful surgery
Fluid collects in cystic spaces within the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers of the fovea, producing a petalloid pattern
A frequent cause is cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), typically peaking a few weeks to months after the operation
Other causes include diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, uveitis, and epiretinal membrane traction
Optical coherence tomography is the key non-invasive test and shows intraretinal cysts and increased central thickness
Fluorescein angiography demonstrates the classic petalloid leakage and often disc staining
Management principles include topical anti-inflammatory therapy for post-surgical cases and treating the underlying vascular or inflammatory driver
Prevention and prompt treatment matter because prolonged oedema can cause permanent photoreceptor loss
reference.pathophysiology: Cystoid macular oedema results from breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, allowing fluid to accumulate in cystic spaces of the macula. Inflammatory mediators, particularly prostaglandins and vascular endothelial growth factor, increase perifoveal capillary permeability. After cataract surgery the trigger is a self-limiting inflammatory response, whereas in diabetes and vein occlusion it reflects chronic vascular incompetence and ischaemia. Vitreomacular traction and epiretinal membranes can contribute mechanically. Sustained fluid accumulation distorts and eventually damages photoreceptors.
additionalDifferentials: Macular oedema from retinal vein occlusion
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography to confirm intraretinal cysts and quantify central macular thickness
Fluorescein angiography to demonstrate petalloid leakage when the diagnosis is uncertain
Dilated fundus examination to identify the underlying vascular or inflammatory cause
Review of surgical and drug history including prostaglandin analogue use
Systemic evaluation for diabetes or vascular disease where relevant
redFlags: Progressive central vision loss despite treatment suggesting chronic or refractory oedema
Bilateral oedema pointing to an underlying systemic or inflammatory disorder
New oedema with signs of active uveitis needing evaluation for infective or immune causes
Coexisting neovascularisation threatening haemorrhage or detachment
reference.prognosis: Post-surgical cystoid macular oedema often resolves with anti-inflammatory treatment and a good visual outcome, but oedema secondary to diabetes, vein occlusion, or chronic uveitis tends to recur and can cause lasting central visual impairment if fluid persists.
pitfalls: Missing subtle oedema on clinical examination and delaying an OCT that would confirm it
Attributing poor post-cataract vision to refractive error rather than macular oedema
Overlooking a prostaglandin analogue glaucoma drop as a contributing factor
Failing to treat the underlying vascular or inflammatory cause and treating only the fluid
management: Treat post-surgical (Irvine-Gass) oedema with topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drops combined with topical corticosteroids to counter prostaglandin-driven leakage
Escalate persistent or refractory cases to periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid therapy
Give intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor agents and consider laser for oedema secondary to diabetic retinopathy or retinal vein occlusion
Control any underlying uveitis with anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapy directed at the primary disease
Discontinue prostaglandin analogue glaucoma drops if implicated as a trigger
Consider vitrectomy where vitreomacular traction or an epiretinal membrane is mechanically contributing
Monitor response with optical coherence tomography to track central macular thickness and resolution of intraretinal cysts
